## Summary (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君)

The standard, full biography of [玄奘](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%84%E5%A5%98) (Xuánzàng, 602–664) — the great Táng pilgrim, translator, and founder of the Dharma-Characters (Fǎxiàng / Yogācāra) school — in ten juan, composed by his disciple [慧立](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%85%A7%E7%AB%8B) (Huìlì) in the years immediately after Xuánzàng's death and supplemented decades later by [彥悰](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BD%A5%E6%82%B0) (Yàncóng of Cí'ēnsì, not to be confused with the Suí translator or the disciple of [法琳](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B3%95%E7%90%B3)). [彥悰](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BD%A5%E6%82%B0) is reported to have completed the supplementation in 688, presenting the text to the throne at that time. This is one of the foundational documents of medieval Chinese Buddhism and the principal source for Xuánzàng's life, his Indian journey, and his Cháng'ān translation activity.

**Abstract**

The structure follows the canonical East Asian Buddhist biographical form, expanded to ten juan. Juan 1 covers Xuánzàng's birth, family, and entry into the saṃgha. Juan 2–5 give the overland journey to India through Central Asia (629–631), the years at Nālandā monastery (635–642), the southern Indian itinerary, and the return journey (643–645). Juan 6–10 cover the Cháng'ān years (645–664): the imperial reception by Tàizōng, the establishment of the translation bureau at Hóngfú-sì 弘福寺 and then Dà Cí'ēn-sì 大慈恩寺, the great translations of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* in 600 juan, and the Abhidharma corpus, and finally the death at Yùhuá-gōng 玉華宮 in 664.

[慧立](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%85%A7%E7%AB%8B) composed the original draft (the *běn* 本) shortly after Xuánzàng's death, but the completed work was buried with him at his death. [彥悰](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BD%A5%E6%82%B0) retrieved the manuscript, expanded it with annotations and supplementary documents (the *jiān* 箋 / 箋注), and presented the completed work in 688 (Wǔ Zétiān *Chuígǒng* 垂拱 4). The combined text is the most detailed biography of any Chinese Buddhist monk before the Sòng.

The biography contains the only extant detailed narrative of Xuánzàng's overland journey, his interactions with the Central Asian and Indian polities (including King Harṣavardhana of Kanyakubja), his debates at Indian monastic universities, and his philosophical disputes with non-Buddhist scholars. It is the principal source for the geography of seventh-century Buddhist India as seen by an East Asian eyewitness — supplementary to Xuánzàng's own *Dà Táng xīyù jì* 大唐西域記 ([KR6t0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6t/KR6t0011)).
